# Sendlyr

> Sendlyr helps product teams validate whether a candidate behavior is real and whether driving it moves the outcome.

## Primary pages

- [Home](https://sendlyr.com/): Signal Validation Pilot overview and qualification.
- [How it works](https://sendlyr.com/how-it-works): Candidate behavior, controlled experiment, and readout method.
- [Typesy VIP case study](https://sendlyr.com/blog/pai-discovery-case-study): Corrected controlled experiment, including a null trial-conversion result.
- [Edtech apps](https://sendlyr.com/for/edtech-apps): Edtech signal-validation use case.

## Public evidence boundary

In eReflect's Typesy VIP experiment, the leading indicator—completing at least one course within the first four days—was 69.4% (129/186) in treatment and 57.7% (56/97) in control. The difference was +11.7 percentage points and +20.3% relative, with z ≈ 1.95 and p ≈ 0.051: borderline, not clean statistical significance.

Trial conversion was 76.8% (136/177) in treatment and 76.7% (66/86) in control, a +0.1 percentage-point difference. There is no conversion lift. A ceiling effect is the leading explanation for the null because roughly 77% of control trials converted without the intervention, leaving little headroom.

Within the unexposed control arm, indicator hitters converted at 75.5% (n=49) versus 78.4% (n=37) for non-hitters. The indicator did not predict conversion in that comparison. The confidence interval is roughly −21 percentage points to +15 percentage points, so a moderate effect cannot be ruled out.

Only the two intent-to-treat comparisons are interpretable. The treatment/no-hit subgroup cross-tab is not reported because `pai_hit` is post-treatment; conditioning on it breaks randomization through collider bias. These results do not establish revenue lift, conversion lift, or that completing a course caused conversion.
